frames.narration: Six connection attempts arrive at a server that listens on 443, 22 and 5432. Three are for 443 or the database from allowed places. The first rule set is a stateless ACL that allows 443 from anywhere and 5432 from 10.0.0.0/16, with no outbound rules.

The requests pass: 3 reach the server. But the replies go back from port 443 to the client's port 50000, and a stateless filter sees them as new packets with no allowing rule. They are dropped. 0 connections work and the clients just time out.

Add one outbound rule for ports 1024 to 65535 and the same three requests now complete: 3 connections work. Switch to a stateful security group with the same inbound rules and no outbound rule at all, and the result is the same, because the connection table lets the replies through.

Order matters in an ACL. Put 'deny 203.0.113.0/24' first and only 2 connections work, because the deny wins before the 443 allow is reached. Put it second and 3 work. Same rules, different list order.

Now the trap: to test something, someone allows all ports from 0.0.0.0/0. 5 of 6 connections work, including SSH on 22 and the database on 5432 from the internet. Nothing breaks, so nobody removes it. Reachability is now the whole internet.

Outbound, a private host cannot be reached by address, so its traffic goes through the NAT gateway. 10.0.2.10:40001 becomes 198.51.100.1:1024 and the pair is stored. A reply to port 1025 is rewritten back to 10.0.2.11:40001; a packet to port 9999 matches no entry and is dropped.

The table is finite. The toy pool holds 20 ports. 4 new connections per tick held for 3 ticks peak at 12 in use and drop nothing. Held for 6 ticks they need 24, the pool pins at 20, and 20 connections are dropped over 30 ticks.

A second public address doubles the pool to 40. The same load peaks at 24 and drops nothing. Shorter timeouts or reusing connections would also cut the need; both are cheaper than more addresses when the cause is idle holds.
